title: $28 B Hemp‑THC Industry Battles Looming Federal Ban, Fights for Survival
body:
The U.S. House of Representatives has voted to close a decades‑old loophole that has allowed hemp‑derived THC products to operate in a legal gray area, a move that could upend a $28 billion industry built on “hemp‑derived” cannabinoids. Lawmakers argue the amendment will tighten enforcement of the Controlled Substances Act and prevent the sale of products that contain more than the federally permitted 0.3 percent delta‑9 THC. Producers, investors and state regulators warn that the change could cripple a rapidly expanding market that has generated jobs, tax revenue and new consumer categories ranging from gummies to beverages.

The contested provision, part of the 2023 Farm Bill, created a carve‑out for “hemp” that could be cultivated and processed without a DEA license, provided the plant’s delta‑9 THC level stayed below the 0.3 percent threshold. In practice, many manufacturers have used sophisticated extraction and formulation techniques to produce products that deliver intoxicating effects while still meeting the letter of the law. The House vote—92 to 31—aims to redefine “hemp” to exclude any product that can be converted into delta‑9 THC, effectively forcing companies to either reformulate their offerings or cease operations.

Industry leaders say the proposed rule change threatens the livelihood of thousands of workers and could push the market underground. In a commercial kitchen on the outskirts of Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns, co‑founder of a boutique edibles brand, demonstrates the painstaking process of creating a signature THC‑infused gummy. The blue‑green “goo” he spreads into a gridded mold is the result of a multi‑step extraction that isolates a high‑potency cannabinoid blend while keeping the raw hemp under the legal limit. “We’re not just making candy; we’re building a supply chain that includes farmers, processors, packaging firms and retailers,” Hohns said. “If the loophole disappears, the entire ecosystem collapses.”

State regulators have been grappling with the disparity between federal guidance and local enforcement. Several states, including Colorado and Oregon, have already established licensing frameworks for hemp‑derived THC products, treating them similarly to traditional cannabis. These states argue that a blanket federal ban would undermine their ability to collect taxes, enforce safety standards and protect consumers. Conversely, law‑enforcement groups and some congressional members contend that the current loophole enables the proliferation of products that can cause intoxication, especially among minors, and creates confusion for law‑abiding businesses that must navigate a patchwork of state rules.

Investors are also feeling the pressure. Venture capital flowing into hemp‑derived THC startups surged to an estimated $2 billion in 2023, driven by consumer demand for “legal highs” that avoid the stigma of recreational marijuana. If the amendment becomes law, many of these firms could see valuations plummet, prompting a wave of consolidations or exits. Some analysts predict a shift in capital toward fully regulated cannabis markets, where licensing is clearer and the risk of federal intervention lower.

The House vote is only the first step; the measure now heads to the Senate, where bipartisan support appears less certain. Lawmakers are expected to weigh the economic benefits of a thriving hemp‑derived sector against public‑health concerns and the desire for a uniform drug policy. Meanwhile, companies like Hohns’ are racing to adapt, exploring alternative cannabinoids such as delta‑8, delta‑10 and CBG, or redesigning products to meet stricter THC limits.

What lies ahead will hinge on whether Congress can craft a compromise that preserves the legitimate hemp industry while addressing the legitimate concerns about potency and safety. For now, the industry watches the legislative process closely, aware that the outcome could reshape the landscape of legal cannabinoids in the United States for years to come.
